body.text: As Vietnam enters its “era of national rise,” a socioeconomic blueprint for transforming Vietnam into a “democratic, fair, and civilized society,” there are growing expectations that marginalized groups such as the country’s LGBTQ+ community will attract attention from the forward-looking government led by President and Communist Party chief To Lam. Many base their hopes for the legalization of same-sex marriages on economic logic, arguing that social inclusion can contribute to Vietnam’s overall national development agenda through the engagement of LGBTQ+ individuals in family-oriented markets.
The prospect of Vietnam recognizing same-sex marriages in the near future, however, remains slim.

To evaluate the growth of Vietnam’s LGBTQ+ community and the extent to which the government tolerates this group, Pride events offer a useful indicator. Since its inception in 2012, VietPride has held a series of events, such as film screenings, workshops, and public rallies, and, at one point, expanded to more than 30 cities and provinces across the country. This year’s Pride events were held in Hanoi, Vietnam’s capital, and Ho Chi Minh City, its largest city, from September 26 to October 4, embodying the most dynamic activities of the LGBTQ+ community.

However, compared with the corresponding festivals in countries such as Taiwan and Thailand, Vietnam’s Pride events have largely remained confined to indoor venues. In a setback for the Vietnamese LGBTQ+ community, it was unable to hold its Pride parade with a giant rainbow flag in downtown Ho Chi Minh City, marking the second consecutive year in which this prominent symbol of the LGBTQ+ community has been absent from Pride events in public spaces.

The absence of Pride parades diminishes the visibility of the LGBTQ+ community in the country, for these events provide a vital platform for members and advocates to show their presence in society and fight for equality.

What exactly caused the cancellation of the public Pride parade remains unclear. But its absence coincides with a broader tightening of state control over civil society and a far-reaching crackdown on independent labor unions and human rights advocates.

Some observers have attributed the ban to Vietnamese authorities’ fear of growing youth-led protests across Asia. VietPride organizers cited “unprecedented pressure on individuals and groups involved in the events,” from online spaces to the real-life environment, as the reason for the cancellation of the 2025 Pride parade. Given the government’s long-standing tolerance of the LGBTQ+ movement, the absence of the flagship Pride march raises serious questions about Vietnam’s commitment to LGBTQ+ equal rights, despite prior breakthroughs regarding LGBTQ+ inclusivity.

Looking back at 2015, when Vietnam symbolically abolished its ban on same-sex marriage but fell short of full recognition. Same-sex couples can cohabit and hold public wedding ceremonies, but their marriage is not legally recognized with a marriage certificate. LGBTQ+ members and human rights activists were overly optimistic in expecting their right to marry to be soon recognized by law. This watershed moment, which was followed by the legal recognition of transgender people, attracted international attention, with many Western outlets even calling Vietnam a leader in gay rights in Asia. Nevertheless, that momentum quickly faded as the government turned its attention to economic priorities, such as foreign direct investment, economic growth, and laws on public investment.

Consequently, the legal limbo of “no prohibition, but no recognition” regarding same-sex marriage has remained in place for more than a decade, leaving Vietnam trailing Taiwan and Thailand in regional LGBTQ+ rights progress. To make matters worse, the ambiguous outcome has been used as a pretext by a minority of the population to oppose the legalization of same-sex marriage and undermine the LGBTQ+ community’s struggle for equality. Conservatives argue that since the government no longer prohibits same-sex couples from tying the knot, LGBTQ+ couples should simply live their lives like their heterosexual counterparts rather than “making a fuss” (làm quá) by repeatedly demanding equal rights. These stereotypical arguments reflect the persistent stigma and discrimination toward LGBTQ+ people.

Despite relentless efforts from the Vietnamese LGBTQ+ movement for social inclusion and recognition, the legalization of same-sex marriage seems to be an issue that the government is deliberately sidestepping. For example, a viral online campaign led by the Institute for Social, Economic and Environmental Research (iSEE) encouraged people to participate in last year’s public consultation on constitutional amendments. The iSEE campaign advocated for revisions to Article 26 (on gender equality) and Article 36 (on marriage and family), “with the aim of ensuring inclusion of individuals belonging to minority groups in terms of sexual orientation and gender identity.”

However, the government proceeded with the constitutional amendments without taking their views into account, a result that disappointed the LGBTQ+ community. Similarly, a few Vietnamese lawmakers have spoken out strongly in support of LGBTQ+ people, including the recent proposal to allow two parents of the same gender to be included on their children’s birth certificates. However, their voices have failed to gain traction within the National Assembly, despite the unprecedented number of laws and regulations passed recently.

These prominent examples demonstrate that Vietnam’s nuanced approach toward LGBTQ+ issues could be framed as a strategy of gradualism. The country opts for a “slow and steady” approach to supporting LGBTQ+ rights instead of pursuing revolutionary change, which the government may perceive as potentially provoking a social backlash. In Vietnam, a society with deeply ingrained Confucian values, the patriarchal family ideal remains dominant while heterosexual families are viewed as the core “cell” (tế bào) of society, rendering the Vietnamese government careful and calculated in navigating LGBTQ+ rights issues. To push back European countries’ concerns over its human rights record, the Vietnamese government accommodates the demands of the LGBTQ+ community to an extent that does not provoke a public backlash. In general, it focuses on lifting restrictions instead of granting new rights.

In stark contrast to the government’s “take-it-slow” approach, Vietnamese society has incrementally become tolerant of same-sex relationships. A survey by the United Nations Development Programme in 2025 found that 65 percent of respondents expressed support for same-sex marriage, which is a marked increase from 37 percent in 2013. At the same time, the LGBTQ+ movement has received significant public support, with its major events and campaigns attracting substantial participation, especially from homosexual people and parents of LGBTQ+ children, demonstrating a strong demand for marriage equality and social inclusion. Social discourse regarding LGBTQ+ issues has significantly improved, partly due to media coverage that positively reflects the real stories of LGBTQ+ individuals.

As the country is heading toward a socioeconomic leap with a firm embrace of the notion of “leaving no one behind,” LGBTQ+ people can no longer afford to be ignored and excluded from that progress. Operating on the assumption that economic growth and political stability come first – while the rights of LGBTQ+ individuals can be addressed later – risks creating a situation in which LGBTQ+ people are repeatedly left behind. In other words, economic growth cannot guarantee political activism and social inclusion if LGBTQ+ people continue to be excluded from legal protections and exposed to discrimination.

Essentially, true progress requires concrete actions from the government in consultation with social organizations and non-governmental organizations advocating for LGBTQ+ rights. Any step toward a legal framework and social inclusion for LGBTQ+ people must be accompanied by educational initiatives and community dialogues that raise awareness of their rights and reduce stigma against them. But for this marginalized community, the path towards legal equality and institutional support is likely to remain a long one.
